claims.text: The initial material is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with nominal TaVCrW composition.
Replacing the empirical EAM potential with a high-fidelity MTP for the liquid phase will retain accurate fusion-property estimates.
Replacing thermodynamic integration with free-energy perturbation will substantially reduce computational cost.
The MTP will be trained to reproduce ab initio phase-space distributions.
FEP will be used to evaluate both solid-state and liquid-state free energies.
The proposed calculations use GGA-PBE and LDA at 0 GPa over 2000–2400 K.
MTP training and molecular dynamics use a 12×12×12 supercell containing approximately 3456 atoms.
The MTP can reproduce the ab initio configuration space with training errors below 1 meV/atom.
Sub-meV/atom MTP training errors ensure sufficiently accurate statistical sampling for FEP.
The MTP enables efficient phase-space sampling.
The MTP reduces the variance of energy differences between DFT and MTP.
Reduced DFT–MTP energy-difference variance allows FEP to converge rapidly.
The method captures electronic Gibbs-energy differences associated with a density-of-states gap.
Solid-state short-range order provides approximately 2.4 meV/atom of stabilization.
The MTP-FEP workflow will reduce computational resource use by approximately 80% relative to TOR-TILD.
The MTP-FEP workflow will be approximately 20 times faster than TOR-TILD.
MTP-FEP free-energy differences will remain within 0.5 meV/atom of traditional TI results.
Electronic excitations will cause melting-temperature shifts of 48–57 K.
The original TOR-TILD baseline uses two EAM potentials, ab initio molecular dynamics, and thermodynamic integration.
Applicability is bounded to multicomponent BCC refractory alloys at 0 GPa and 2000–2400 K.

contradictions.description: An 80% reduction in resource usage corresponds to about a 5× improvement for an otherwise equivalent workload, not the simultaneously claimed 20× speedup, which would correspond to about a 95% reduction.
